records.title: Chromatic pavilions and modular play structures activate historic Istanbul Rami Library
records.dek: Milimetrik Architects turned Istanbul's Rami Library into an eleven-day family festival of open-ended play spaces and house-shaped book-fair pavilions, welcoming around 825,000 visitors.
summary: For AileFest 2026, Turkish practice Milimetrik Architects adapted the historic Rami Library's courtyard and interior halls into a 91,000-sqm connected landscape for family recreation, education and culture.
The courtyard avoids fixed play equipment, offering modular geometric volumes, abstract shelters and colourful gathering nodes sized for different age groups and open to spontaneous use.

Inside, the book fair replaces standard booth grids with pitched house-shaped pavilions, primary-coloured stands and graphic floors, all built in temporary timber and steel that leaves the heritage fabric untouched.
records.why: For Community and Retail, it shows how a family weekend event or a school-holiday mall visit can be staged as one connected play-and-culture landscape using temporary, reversible structures. It also offers Education a fresh template for the school book fair.
records.excerpt: Instead of prescribing how children should play, the designers supplied abstract volumes and shelters and let families decide how to use them.
records.oppText: Residents find a community park or plaza temporarily filled with timber-and-steel pavilions that link open play areas with reading corners and cultural programming over a festival week.

opps.title: Neighbourhood family festival
opps.text: Residents find a community park or plaza temporarily filled with timber-and-steel pavilions that link open play areas with reading corners and cultural programming over a festival week.

opps.title: Holiday atrium play landscape
opps.text: Families visiting a mall during school holidays encounter modular geometric volumes and colourful gathering nodes in the atrium, sized for different ages and free to use however children choose.

opps.title: House-shaped book fair
opps.text: Students and parents browse the school book fair through pitched house-shaped pavilions, primary-coloured stands and graphic floor patterns rather than rows of trestle tables.

keyInsights: Temporary timber-and-steel structures can activate a heritage or civic site for families without altering its fabric.
Replacing rigid play equipment with modular, abstract volumes leaves room for spontaneous use across different age groups.
A familiar format such as a book fair can be reorganised with house-shaped pavilions, primary colours and floor graphics instead of standard booth rows.
Continuous circulation between outdoor and indoor zones allows one event to hold recreation, education and culture together.

_bench.title: Play Without a Script
_bench.short: AileFest 2026 filled Istanbul's Rami Library with modular play volumes and house-shaped book-fair pavilions for an eleven-day family festival.
_bench.lead: Families move between an outdoor courtyard of modular geometric volumes, abstract shelters and colourful gathering nodes and indoor halls where the book fair is arranged in house-shaped pavilions. Circulation between the courtyard and the historic galleries is continuous, and the play elements are sized ergonomically for children of different ages.

why.head: Open-ended over prescriptive
why.body: Abstract volumes and shelters replace fixed play equipment, allowing spontaneous use and open circulation.

why.head: Scaled for every age
why.body: The spatial design is built around ergonomic scales for varying age groups rather than a single user.

why.head: Heritage left intact
why.body: Temporary timber-and-steel fabrications activate the civic site without altering its historic fabric.

transfer.how: Stage a school-holiday atrium of modular, brightly coloured play volumes sized for different ages instead of a single branded play set.
Redesign the school book fair with house-shaped pavilions, primary-coloured stands and graphic floors in place of standard booth rows.
Create a seasonal family courtyard at a resort using reversible timber-and-steel shelters and gathering nodes that leave the permanent landscape untouched.

records.title: Disney Adventure
records.dek: Disney Cruise Line reworked an unfinished mega-ship into a set of story-led areas, treating the vessel itself as the destination rather than the means of travel.
summary: Disney Cruise Line acquired a partially built vessel in 2022 and spent more than three years reimagining it as Disney Adventure, its largest ship, with 20 decks and room for up to 6,700 guests.

The ship centres on Disney Imagination Garden, an open-air gathering space with the first castle at sea, surrounded by six further themed areas such as Marvel Landing and San Fransokyo Street, which between them offer water play, themed dining, outdoor entertainment and interactive attractions.

Live programming carries much of the experience, from shows at a Garden Stage framed by three-deck-high LED screens to an original theatre production and a Moana performance staged around a pool with amphitheatre-style seating, supported by six rotational dining venues and partner brands including Bacha Coffee and TWG Tea.
records.why: For Retail, it shows how a large destination can be broken into named, story-led areas so a family's mall visit feels like moving between worlds rather than along corridors. For Community, it shows how a central open-air gathering space with staged performances can become the heart of neighbourhood life.
records.excerpt: The themed areas are built to be used, not admired: across them guests find water play, dining, entertainment and attractions rather than scenery alone.
records.oppText: Shoppers move through distinct, named quarters of a mall, each with its own architecture, family play element and themed dining, so a visit has a clear sense of journey.

opps.title: Story-led mall quarters
opps.text: Shoppers move through distinct, named quarters of a mall, each with its own architecture, family play element and themed dining, so a visit has a clear sense of journey.

opps.title: Poolside story evenings

opps.title: Central garden stage

keyInsights: Breaking a very large venue into a handful of named, themed areas makes it easier to navigate and gives visitors places to aim for.
Themed spaces earn their keep when they double as working venues for play, dining and entertainment rather than serving as backdrops.
Live performance placed in open gathering spaces, not only in theatres, creates shared moments across a whole destination.
Partner brands and first-of-their-kind shops can lift the premium feel of a destination without the operator building everything itself.

_bench.title: A Ship Organised Into Story Worlds
_bench.short: Disney Adventure divides a 6,700-guest ship into a central open-air garden and six named themed areas, together hosting play, dining, entertainment and attractions.
_bench.lead: Guests move between distinct story worlds such as Toy Story Place, Marvel Landing with the longest roller coaster at sea, and San Fransokyo Street, rather than between generic decks. Live shows anchor the shared spaces, from the Garden Stage with its three-deck-high LED screens to a Moana performance around a pool with amphitheatre-style seating.

why.head: Scale made legible
why.body: A central garden and six named areas give a 20-deck ship a clear structure that families can navigate and look forward to.

why.head: Spaces built to be used
why.body: The themed areas function as play, dining, entertainment and attraction venues rather than decoration.

why.head: Shows anchor gathering spaces
why.body: Open-air stage and poolside performances turn shared areas into collective moments for families.

transfer.how: Organise a large mall into a few named, themed quarters, each pairing distinctive design with family play and dining so visitors have places to head for.
Create a central open-air gathering space in a community with a permanent stage for regular family performances.
Give school campuses named, story-led zones for play and learning so younger students and parents can find their way and feel a sense of place.

records.title: Clash for the Stache: turning a mobile game into a real-world entertainment experience
records.dek: Supercell and GDX Studios turned Clash of Clans into an eight-week, actor-led physical adventure in San Diego that worked for committed fans and first-timers alike.
summary: Timed to San Diego Comic-Con, Supercell and GDX Studios staged an eight-week immersive experience at Seaport Headquarters in which visitors became Chiefs on a mission to recover the Barbarian's stolen moustache.

Live actors, physical challenge rooms, interactive puzzles, cooperative games, photo moments and an exclusive retail space were woven into one narrative, with set details checked repeatedly against the original game artwork.
The design was layered so newcomers and families could join easily while long-standing fans found depth, and surveyed guests reported high satisfaction and recommendation scores.
records.why: For Retail and Community, it shows how a mall visit or a neighbourhood event can become a story guests step into, with actors and layered challenges that suit families and first-timers as well as devotees. The layering approach is a practical model for any seasonal destination activation.
records.excerpt: The aim was to let guests feel they had walked into the game's world, not to rebuild a video game in physical form.
records.oppText: Shoppers join a seasonal, actor-guided quest through themed challenge rooms in the mall, with puzzles pitched for both children and returning fans and a story-linked retail corner.

opps.title: Mall-wide story quest
opps.text: Shoppers join a seasonal, actor-guided quest through themed challenge rooms in the mall, with puzzles pitched for both children and returning fans and a story-linked retail corner.

opps.title: Neighbourhood adventure weekends
opps.text: Residents' families take on cooperative team challenges across the public realm, led by costumed characters who give every participant a role in a shared story.

opps.title: Resort family storyline
opps.text: Young guests receive a character role on arrival and complete live-actor challenges around the resort during their stay, with depth that rewards returning families.

keyInsights: Giving visitors a role in the story turns spectators into participants and deepens emotional connection.
Layering content lets one experience satisfy newcomers and dedicated fans at the same time.
Authenticity lives in small details, from textures to finishes, checked repeatedly against the source world.
Sound, touch and live performance make a space feel believable beyond visual recognition.

It was to make guests feel as though they had entered the Clash of Clans world itself.')

_bench.title: Stepping Inside the Story
_bench.short: For eight weeks in San Diego, visitors became characters in a live-acted Clash of Clans quest to recover a stolen moustache.
_bench.lead: Guests were cast as Chiefs and guided by live actors, including the Archer Queen, through physical challenge rooms, interactive puzzles and cooperative team games. The journey also included photo moments and an exclusive retail environment, with layered detail so newcomers and long-time fans could each engage at their own level.

why.head: Guests become participants
why.body: A clear mission and an assigned role turn passive viewing into active play.

why.head: Layered for every audience
why.body: Simple entry points welcome families and first-timers while hidden depth rewards devoted fans.

why.head: Obsessive authenticity
why.body: Proportions, textures, finishes and even studs and screws were checked against the original artwork.

transfer.how: Community events could cast residents' families as characters in a cooperative, actor-led challenge across shared amenities.
Resorts could give children a story role at check-in and stage live character challenges throughout the stay.
Schools could run open days as narrative quests where prospective students solve team puzzles guided by staff in character.

records.title: Gravity Haus wants to make mountain life a membership
records.dek: A mountain hospitality brand bundles rooms, workspaces and gyms into tiered memberships, serving the busy parent who wants a day on the slopes without needing a bed.
summary: Gravity Haus, founded by Jim Deters, now lists 13 properties across the western US and British Columbia, each combining hotel rooms, workspaces and gyms in outdoor destinations.
Its clearest use case is a parent who drives up for the day, drops the children at ski school and uses the property as a base to work, ski, train, eat and wait out the traffic before driving home.

Memberships start at an annual entry tier with lodging discounts, and higher property, network and seasonal tiers add access without an overnight stay, though the model depends on renewals, repeat visits and on-property spending.
records.why: For Hospitality and Community, it shows how a venue can become a day base for a resident or visiting family, covering work, exercise, meals and children's activities, rather than serving only the overnight stay.
records.excerpt: The property shapes almost every part of the family's day while earning from a visitor who doesn't always need a bed - Colin Nagy's account of the day-use member.
records.oppText: A non-staying family member buys a day pass that bundles a desk, gym access, a meal and a place to wait while the children attend a resort activity programme.

opps.text: A non-staying family member buys a day pass that bundles a desk, gym access, a meal and a place to wait while the children attend a resort activity programme.

opps.title: Neighbourhood Haus Membership
opps.text: Residents join a tiered membership that brings together co-working, fitness and family amenities in one community hub, with higher tiers unlocking partner hospitality perks.

keyInsights: Designing around the time-constrained parent or professional, not the hardcore enthusiast, widens who a destination serves.
Day-use access lets a property earn from people who never book a room while becoming part of their routine.
Tiered memberships can create a sense of belonging across a network, but only if renewals and repeat use justify the discounts and facilities.
Bundling familiar purchases into one unfamiliar fee requires clear explanation for customers to grasp the value.

records.title: Alaska Airlines flagship lounge by Graham Baba Architects
records.dek: At Seattle-Tacoma, Alaska Airlines trades lounge exclusivity for warmth, with a staged entry and four mood-based zones rooted in the Pacific Northwest.
summary: Alaska Airlines set out to reinvent the airport lounge as a welcoming home-away-from-home rather than a sleek, exclusive business enclave, with Graham Baba Architects designing its flagship at SeaTac.

The space is organised into four zones named for how guests want to feel (an approachable entry, a casual bistro, a quiet relaxation area and a lively bar), each with its own furniture, acoustics, materials and light, and lightly divided by oak and metal screens.
A choreographed approach from the concourse, a central fireplace, sweeping runway and mountain views, and custom pieces by local fabricators give the lounge a distinct sense of the Seattle region.
records.why: For Hospitality and Retail, the lounge shows how an arrival sequence and mood-named zones can let every guest find their own place within a single venue, whether in a hotel lobby or a mall visitor lounge. It also shows how local makers can give a space a felt sense of where you are.
records.excerpt: Rather than signalling privilege, the lounge is designed so that each guest can find a corner that feels like home, whether they want quiet, food, work or company.
records.oppText: Hotel guests move from a welcoming entry into distinct, lightly screened zones for eating, resting and socialising, each with its own lighting, acoustics and furniture.

opps.title: Lobby of four moods
opps.text: Hotel guests move from a welcoming entry into distinct, lightly screened zones for eating, resting and socialising, each with its own lighting, acoustics and furniture.

opps.title: Mall refuge lounge
opps.text: Shoppers step off a busy concourse into a calm, low-lit lounge with recliners and sound-absorbing finishes, glimpsed through a large window before they enter.

opps.title: Local makers clubhouse
opps.text: Residents gather in a community clubhouse furnished with lighting, screens and fixtures made by regional fabricators, creating a visible connection to the place they live.

keyInsights: Naming zones after how people want to feel, rather than by function, helps guests choose the experience that suits them.
A staged approach of glimpses, guiding frames and a focal point such as a fireplace turns entry into an invitation.
Varying acoustics, light and materials between zones lets one venue serve families, solo travellers and groups at once.
Commissioning local fabricators builds a sense of place that generic premium finishes cannot.

It is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote.)

_bench.title: One Lounge, Four Ways to Feel
_bench.short: Alaska Airlines' SeaTac flagship lounge is split into four zones (Come In, Help Yourself, Take a Breath, Cut Loose) for different guest moods.
_bench.lead: Guests pass a welcoming entry and concierge, then choose between a central bistro, a dimmed relaxation area with recliners and banquettes, or a convivial bar. Each zone has its own furnishings, acoustics, floor and ceiling materials and light, separated only by oak and twisted metal screens so the spaces flow together.

why.head: Welcome replaces exclusivity
why.body: The lounge is conceived as a warm refuge for all guests rather than a sleek enclave for a privileged few.

why.head: Zones named for feelings
why.body: Labels such as Take a Breath and Cut Loose tell guests what each space is for, so they can find where they feel at home.

why.head: Local makers, real place
why.body: Custom lighting, screens and fixtures by local fabricators and artists connect guests to the Seattle region and the airline's West Coast heritage.

transfer.how: A mall visitor lounge could offer distinct quiet, café and social zones with different lighting and acoustics, lightly screened rather than walled off.
Community clubhouses could be zoned by mood, from a calm reading corner to a lively social bar, and furnished with pieces by regional makers.
School reception areas could pair an approachable concierge-style welcome with separate calm and social waiting spaces for parents and families.

records.title: Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw
records.dek: A creative director, a DJ and an architect have turned the ground floor of a post-war office block into a music-first venue rooted in Rotterdam's port and club culture.
summary: Echo, a listening bar opposite Rotterdam Centraal, was conceived by Jeff Hoogendijk, Khalil Ryahi and Paul Cournet after visits to Tokyo listening bars, and puts the experience of music at the centre of a flexible space.

Its main bar, which doubles as service counter and DJ booth, was built with a wooden shipping-crate maker as a nod to the city's seaport, carries the tagline 'handled with care', and sits among ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis and vinyl shelving fitted with a Tylko and Form Follows Frequency speaker system.

The venue moves from coffee shop by day to bar by night, adds curated retail, hosts exhibitions, listening sessions and seated dinners, and has invited local record stores to shape its event programme.
records.why: For Aldar's F&B outlets and mall destinations, Echo shows how a single venue can serve a morning coffee visit and an evening music event while drawing its identity from local materials and local creative communities.
records.excerpt: "We wanted to make it super local." - Paul Cournet
records.oppText: Guests move from a daytime coffee bar to an evening vinyl session in the same lounge, with a carefully tuned sound system and small-capacity listening events for 20 to 40 people.

opps.title: Hotel listening lounge
opps.text: Guests move from a daytime coffee bar to an evening vinyl session in the same lounge, with a carefully tuned sound system and small-capacity listening events for 20 to 40 people.

opps.title: Day-to-night music corner
opps.text: Shoppers find a café that becomes a bar after dark, with curated records and objects for sale and a calendar of sessions programmed by local record sellers.

opps.title: Neighbourhood sound sessions
opps.text: Residents attend intimate listening evenings and pop-up exhibitions in a shared community space, with programmes co-curated by local music and creative groups.

keyInsights: Anchoring a venue in local materials and history gives visitors a story they can see and touch, not just a theme.
A space designed to shift between coffee shop, bar, exhibition and dinner venue earns footfall across the whole day.
Inviting local specialists, such as record stores, to programme events builds credibility with the community the venue wants to attract.
Contrasting raw architecture with refined sensory elements like sound and light can make an existing building feel warmer rather than requiring it to be disguised.

_bench.title: A Counter That Tells the City's Story
_bench.short: Echo's main bar, also the DJ area, is built from wooden shipping crates referencing Rotterdam's seaport and printed with the tagline 'handled with care'.
_bench.lead: Guests order drinks and watch the DJ at a single counter made with a shipping-crate manufacturer and a carpenter, a visible reminder that Rotterdam hosts Europe's largest seaport. The crate's printed words 'handled with care' became the venue's tagline, signalling that music and hospitality are treated with equal attention.

why.head: Local identity made physical
why.body: The crate bar turns the city's port heritage into something guests stand at and touch every visit.

why.head: One object, two roles
why.body: Combining the service counter and DJ area puts the music and the hospitality in the same focal point of the room.

why.head: A tagline drawn from design
why.body: Lifting 'handled with care' from the crate gives the brand a promise rooted in its own fabric.

transfer.how: A mall café or concept store could build its central counter with a local craftsperson using a material tied to the area's heritage, explained through a short line printed on the piece.
A community centre's reception or clubhouse bar could be crafted from materials that reference the neighbourhood's history, giving residents a shared story at the point of welcome.

records.title: Hotel review: a daydream come true at Schlosshotel Fiss
records.dek: A family-run five-star in the Tyrol shows how scent, craft, zoned seating and acoustic design let families and couples share one calm Alpine retreat.
summary: Schlosshotel Fiss, an independently owned 135-room ski-in, ski-out hotel in Austria's Tyrol, deliberately caters to families and couples at once, and the reviewer found the result relaxed rather than compromised.

The experience is built on sensory and spatial choices: aromatic pine walls, natural stone softened by wool, staff in regional dress, locally crafted details, and lounge seating that ranges from cocooned corners for couples to banquettes for family groups.

Its 5,000-square-metre wellness area pairs children's slides with secluded hydrotherapy breakout areas, uses sound insulation to keep the pool calm, and is now being extended with a nature-inspired adventure zone for children and teenagers designed with NOA*.
records.why: For Hospitality, it is a working model for the family resort stay, showing how pool and lounge design can serve children and couples in the same space without either feeling crowded out. For Community and Retail, the same zoning and acoustic logic applies to shared amenities and family weekend visits to a destination.
records.excerpt: "We have always made a conscious effort to work with local craftspeople" - Simone Domenig
records.oppText: Families get slides and splash areas while couples retreat to acoustically screened hydrotherapy niches within the same pool hall, each feeling the space was designed for them.

opps.title: Two-tempo pool deck
opps.text: Families get slides and splash areas while couples retreat to acoustically screened hydrotherapy niches within the same pool hall, each feeling the space was designed for them.

opps.title: Landscape-led adventure zone
opps.text: Children and teenagers explore a nature-inspired play landscape in the neighbourhood that offers a different route or challenge each visit rather than a fixed playground.

opps.title: Quiet corners, lively core
opps.text: Shoppers find cocooned, sound-softened seating pockets for adults alongside generous family banquettes in the dining court, so different groups can settle in comfortably.

keyInsights: Serving families and couples together works when zoning and acoustics give each group its own pocket within a shared space.
Scent and natural materials, such as aromatic pine and wool, make a sense of place felt immediately on arrival and in the room.
Working directly with local artisans produces distinctive detail and a credible regional identity.
Children's facilities can be framed as daily discovery rooted in local landscape rather than a conventional play area.

_bench.short: Schlosshotel Fiss lets families and couples share its Aqua Monte Waterworld, using sound insulation and secluded hydrotherapy breakout areas to keep it calm.
_bench.lead: Children use the water slides while couples relax on hydrotherapy loungers in secluded breakout areas off the 37-metre pool, with glass doors opening onto an outdoor pool and garden. Sound insulation keeps the space calm even when many families are using it.

why.head: One venue serves two audiences
why.body: Families and couples use the same waterworld, and the reviewer found the overall ambience relaxed rather than compromised.

why.head: Acoustics protect the calm
why.body: Sound insulation maintains a sense of calm in the pool despite heavy family use.

why.head: Zoning gives each guest a niche
why.body: Slides for children and secluded loungers for adults echo the lounge's mix of cocooned corners and family banquettes.

transfer.how: Community pools and clubhouses could pair children's water play with acoustically treated, secluded adult loungers in the same facility.
Mall family zones could combine active play areas with sound-softened, cocooned seating pockets for adults nearby.

records.title: Why Nespresso brought its loyalty programme back from dormancy
records.dek: Nespresso has revived its early-2000s club in the US, dropping points in favour of behaviour-based rewards, shared experiences and access designed to make members feel part of a community.
summary: Nespresso has relaunched the Nespresso Club in the US, reworking a programme first built around a sense of exclusivity for a much larger and broader espresso audience.

Instead of points, members receive exclusive blends, personalised discounts and access shaped by how they engage, such as trying limited editions or joining barista classes, alongside birthday and anniversary gifts.

A higher Ambassador tier and partner-led experiences, including a Cannes red carpet invitation for European VIPs, sit on top, while the brand stresses that every member should find something that fits them.
records.why: For Retail, it shows how a mall loyalty scheme could reward how shoppers take part, such as attending a workshop, rather than only what they spend during a visit. For Community, the same logic could recognise residents who join neighbourhood events, turning participation into a sense of belonging.
records.excerpt: Nespresso's leadership wants loyalty to reward behaviour and engagement rather than become "another airline points catalog of things and stuff" - Jean-Christophe Jaunin
records.oppText: Shoppers who join an in-mall class or seasonal workshop receive personalised offers and early access linked to the interests they have shown.

opps.title: Rewarded for taking part
opps.text: Shoppers who join an in-mall class or seasonal workshop receive personalised offers and early access linked to the interests they have shown.

opps.title: Access money cannot buy
opps.text: Returning guests who attend a chef demonstration or tasting are invited to a small members-only experience matched to that interest.

opps.title: Neighbours with shared passions
opps.text: Residents who attend community classes are grouped into interest circles and invited to follow-on sessions with others who share the same hobby.

keyInsights: Rewarding behaviour and engagement, not just spend, gives a brand clearer signals about which rewards each customer values.
Loyalty feels like belonging when rewards bring members together around a shared interest rather than offering a generic catalogue.
Top-tier experiences can inspire, but the core programme must stay useful and worthwhile for every member.
Perks that remove friction, such as early access or easier returns, can make customers feel known without expensive gifts.

_bench.title: Rewarding Who You Are, Not What You Spend
_bench.short: Nespresso Club replaces points with exclusive blends and personalised discounts shaped by how members engage with the brand.
_bench.lead: Members earn no points; instead, actions such as trying a limited-edition blend or joining a barista class tell Nespresso which rewards matter to each person, informing personalised discounts and access to exclusive blends. Details such as boutique visits and capsule recycling give the brand further ways to recognise and celebrate how each member interacts with it.

why.head: Behaviour reveals what members value
why.body: Engagement such as classes and limited-edition trials shows the brand which rewards will feel relevant to each member.

why.head: Rewards build shared community
why.body: Perks like seasonal recipe experiences connect members with others who share the same passion.

why.head: Something for every member
why.body: Alongside top-tier invitations, accessible rewards such as recipe demonstrations keep the programme worthwhile for everyone.

transfer.how: Use guests' participation in on-property classes or tastings to shape personalised offers for their next stay.
Recognise residents who take part in community activities with access to interest-based events rather than generic discounts.
Acknowledge parents who join school workshops with invitations to follow-on sessions tied to the topics they engaged with.

records.title: Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
records.dek: A Copenhagen shop for rare and independent books uses modular, mobile furniture and a small red room so it can shift between bookshop, gallery and venue.
summary: Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, designed to work equally as an exhibition gallery, a listening space and a venue for launches and informal gatherings.

Architect Derya Arpac led a deliberately un-Scandinavian interior of cherry and aluminium modular shelving, a zippered leather counter and mobile book trolleys that encourage visitors to move books around.

A 20-square-metre red room provides scope for small events and exhibitions, the artworks on display change as they are sold, and the shop has already hosted a book launch, a curated library for ASICS and a fashion pop-up.
records.why: For Retail, it shows how a single unit can be fitted out so a mall visit meets something different each time, from browsing to a launch or exhibition. For Community, it suggests a model for amenity spaces that host small resident gatherings without a separate venue.
records.excerpt: "We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired." - Derya Arpac
records.oppText: Shoppers find a curated store whose modular shelving and mobile displays reconfigure for a launch, exhibition or brand pop-up, with a small dedicated room for intimate events.

opps.title: The changing curated unit
opps.text: Shoppers find a curated store whose modular shelving and mobile displays reconfigure for a launch, exhibition or brand pop-up, with a small dedicated room for intimate events.

opps.title: Neighbourhood reading room
opps.text: Residents use a clubhouse library with movable book trolleys and a compact event room that hosts local author talks and small exhibitions.

keyInsights: Modular and mobile furniture lets one retail footprint serve several uses without a refit.
A small, distinct room within a shop creates a ready setting for intimate events and exhibitions.
Displays that change, such as art replaced as it sells, keep a space from feeling static.
Hosting brand partners turns a shop into a platform as well as a point of sale.
